budgets.why: A 120 Hz frame is 8.3 ms and the editor is only one part of it, so a repaint must stay far below that, must not allocate and must not depend on the document's size.
Scrolling repaints the viewport on every frame, so it follows the same limits as a plain repaint: far below a 120 Hz frame, allocation-free and independent of the document's size.
Moving the caret and repainting must take at most 1 ms, allocate nothing and not grow with the length of the document.
Moving by a page and repainting must take at most 1 ms, allocate nothing and not grow with the length of the document.
A keystroke and its frame must finish within 1 ms on the reference machine, with bounded allocation and independent of the document's size.
Pressing Enter and drawing the next frame must finish within 1 ms on the reference machine, with bounded allocation and independent of the document's size.
Undoing or redoing an edit and drawing the next frame must finish within 1 ms on the reference machine, with bounded allocation and independent of the document's size.
Pasting 1 MiB and undoing it takes two frames, which must fit within one 60 Hz frame (16 ms) and not depend on the document's size.
This is the window-thread part of opening a file; building the rope and scanning widths belong on the worker, so it must stay small and grow with the file only slowly.
Preparing a reload may scan the text once, so its cost is bounded by a small constant plus a linear term in the document's size.
Re-wrapping after a width change is one linear pass over the text, so its cost is bounded by a small constant plus 1.5 ns per byte.
An open document may keep one copy of its text plus at most half of it again plus 2 MiB of index and view state alive.
Building the rope from a document is one linear pass, so its cost is bounded by a small constant plus 1.5 ns per byte.
Inserting and deleting a character is a local edit, so it must take at most 2 µs, allocate at most 8 KiB and not depend on the document's size.
Line lookups run for every visible row on every frame, so each must take at most 500 ns, allocate nothing and not depend on the document's size.
Mapping an offset to its line runs on every caret and selection update, so it must take at most 500 ns, allocate nothing and not depend on the document's size.
Reading the visible lines happens on every frame, so it must take at most 50 µs, allocate nothing and not depend on the document's size.
Informational: this is what any whole-document copy costs, and no per-keystroke path may use it.
Reading already computed colors for the viewport happens on every frame, so it must take at most 100 µs, allocate nothing and not depend on the document's size.
The first colors after a jump must arrive within one 120 Hz frame (8.3 ms) and not depend on the document's size.
Re-tokenizing the edited line after a keystroke must take at most 0.5 ms regardless of the document's size.
Bringing the tokenizer state of the following lines up to date after a keystroke must take at most 2 ms regardless of the document's size.
The background pass over the whole document must tokenize at least 20 MB/s, which is at most 50 ns per byte.
The first use of a language, including loading its grammar, must finish within 20 ms.
